title: Aggregate I/O window and threadload hedging to cut host syscall/memcpy churn
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: In production traces for small/interactive prompts we observe large amounts of host-side CPU spent in many tiny memcpy/syscall operations and high threadpool wakeup rates. This increases tail latency and reduces overall GPU utilization. Root causes: (1) incremental prefill pieces (KV cache warmups) triggering repeated pinned-buffer copies; (2) scheduler creates many short-lived tasks that contend for work queues; (3) kernel-selection bookkeeping on the host for short sequences involves extra lookup latencies.

Goal: Reduce host syscall & memcpy churn and threadpool contention while preserving or improving p50/p95 response and throughput. Approach: implement an aggregated I/O "window" and token-aware copy-gating that coalesces small prefill writes into a single DMA submission per request (or per short window), and rework threadpool hedging to keep long-lived worker threads pinned with a low-latency handoff. Complement with a light-weight kernel-selection cache keyed by sequence-length-range so we avoid repeated host-side lookups for common short-shot sizes.

Deliverables:
- design doc describing I/O window semantics and API to runtime components
- prototype of a pooled pinned-buffer allocator and batched DMA submitter
- revised threadpool with per-GPU worker lanes and configurable hedging/backoff
- microbench harness and perf dashboard entry
- canary rollout plan and fallback toggle

Metrics to measure:
- syscall count per request (syscalls/request)
- memcpy bytes vs number of memcpy calls
- host CPU% attributable to runtime
- p50/p95/p99 latency for prefill and decode
- GPU utilization and tokens/sec

Acceptance criteria:
- >=30% reduction in host CPU spent in memcpy/syscall paths for small (<64 token) requests
- >=70% reduction in memcpy call count for these requests
- p99 latency increase <= 5% (or improved)
- no regression in throughput for batched workloads

Constraints and non-goals:
- This work does not change the model kernels themselves (no attention algorithm changes) — focus is on host-side plumbing and light kernel-selection caching.
- Avoid invasive ABI changes for existing private deployments; feature behind runtime flag.

Risks:
- Over-coalescing could increase latency for very low-latency single-token requests.
- Pinned buffer explosion if pool sizing is incorrect.
- Thread affinity changes may interact poorly with NUMA on multi-socket hosts.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Spike (3d): microbench to measure syscall/memcpy breakdown per request size and kernel-selection lookup cost. Validate coalescing heuristic parameters.
2) Design (2d): doc with API and pool sizing heuristics + safety limits.
3) Prototype (7d): implement pinned-buffer pool, batched submitter, and lightweight kernel-selection cache (LRU of size/bucket -> kernel choice).
4) Threadpool revamp (5d): implement worker lanes with pause/resume handoff and backoff to prevent thrashing.
5) Bench & iterate (5d): run internal perf harness and iterate on heuristics.
6) PR + review + canary (3d): staged rollout behind flag and retro metrics.

Notes and references:
- Perf dashboard: https://grafana.internal.redwood/prod/runtime/io-churn
- Design doc draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/IO+Window+and+Pinned+Pool
- Spike repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/compare/ENG-153009-io-window
- Related Linear: ENG-93210 (host handoff batching) noted similar goals but different approach; this ticket focuses on syscall and memcpy reduction via I/O windowing and thread hedging.

Open questions:
- Default coalescing window size: 250us vs 1ms? Need perf trade-off.
- Pool sizing policy: per-GPU vs global per-host.
- Kernel-cache eviction policy and durability across restarts.
